# English language teachers’ acceptance of artificial intelligence predicted by AI literacy and intelligent TPACK within an extended TAM framework

instructional practice. This study examined how English language teachers’ AI literacy and Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (Intelligent TPACK) **KEYWORDS** 

AI literacy; intelligent TPACK; 

in uence their acceptance of AI for pedagogical use. A quantitative, cross-sectional sur- technology acceptance vey design was employed with 360 in-service K–12 English language teachers in the Awi model; English language Administration Zone of the Amhara Region, Ethiopia. Validated scales were used to teaching; teacher education; assess AI literacy, Intelligent TPACK, perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness structural equation modeling \[PU\], and AI acceptance. Structural equation modeling results indicated that AI literacy 

signi cantly predicted Intelligent TPACK, PEOU, and AI acceptance, while its e ect on PU was weak. Intelligent TPACK positively in uenced PEOU, PU, and AI acceptance, 

con rming its pivotal mediating role in AI integration. PU emerged as the strongest determinant of AI acceptance, whereas the direct path from PEOU to acceptance was 

non-signi cant. The ndings indicate that teachers’ acceptance of AI is mainly in uenced by AI literacy, Intelligent TPACK, and perceived usefulness rather than ease of use. The 

study underscores the importance of AI literacy initiatives and professional development focused on Intelligent TPACK and AI-supported pedagogy. 

## 1. Introduction 

The integration of Arti cial Intelligence (AI) into education is rede ning how teachers design, deliver, and evaluate learning experiences. In English language education, AI-powered tools such as automated essay scoring systems, intelligent tutoring platforms, and adaptive language learning applications are trans- forming instructional practices and feedback mechanisms (Huang & Zhang, 2025), Pan et al. ([2025)](#appendix-survey-items), (Promma et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). Collectively, these studies suggest that AI has strong potential to improve instructional e ective- ness; however, they also emphasize that successful implementation depends not merely on access to tech- nology, but on teachers’ readiness to integrate AI in pedagogically meaningful and ethically responsible ways (Tzirides et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). This issue is particularly critical in English language teaching, where instructional practices rely heavily on interaction, contextualized feedback, and communicative competence. These tech- nologies hold great promise for personalizing instruction, supporting student autonomy, and enhancing assessment accuracy. However, their successful adoption depends not only on technological availability but also on teachers’ cognitive, pedagogical, and ethical readiness to integrate AI meaningfully and responsibly (Tzirides et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). For English language teachers, whose instructional practices rely heavily on communi- cation, contextual feedback, and learner interaction, understanding the factors that in uence their accep- tance of AI has become a crucial research priority. 

The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) has long served as a foundational framework for predicting users’ adoption of new technologies. Davis (1989) proposed that perceived usefulness (Lim et al., 2026) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) are key determinants of technology acceptance. PU refers to the degree to which a technology enhances professional or instructional performance, while PEOU re ects how e ortless it is to use (Darayseh, 2023; Davis & Granić, 2024; Galimova et al., 2024). Numerous studies have validated TAM in educational contexts (Bergdahl & Sjöberg, [2025;](#informed-consent) Nja et al., 2023; W. Zhang & Hou, [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Nonetheless,

its focus on individual perceptions often overlooks teachers’ professional knowledge and pedagogical con- text, factors particularly salient in AI integration for English language teaching (Li & Manzari, 2025). 

To address this limitation, recent research has incorporated pedagogical knowledge frameworks into technology adoption models. The Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, origi- nally developed by Mishra and Koehler (2006), provides a comprehensive structure for understanding teachers’ knowledge of integrating technology e ectively in subject-speci c teaching. Its AI-related exten- sion, referred to as Intelligent TPACK in this study, captures English language teachers’ ability to design, implement, and assess instruction with AI tools while maintaining pedagogical soundness and ethical sensi- tivity (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Cheng et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2024). This construct not only re ects knowledge integration but also represents a critical determinant of teachers’ technology acceptance and innovation readiness (Batiibwe & Bakkabulindi, [2016)](#informed-consent). 

Alongside Intelligent TPACK, AI literacy (AIL) has emerged as an essential competency that enables teach- ers to understand, evaluate, and responsibly apply AI in their classrooms (C.-Q. Chen, [2025;](#informed-consent) B. Wang et al., [2022)](#appendix-survey-items). AIL encompasses cognitive, technical, and ethical dimensions of AI understanding, skills that empower teachers to interpret AI-generated outputs, recognize algorithmic limitations, and use AI tools appropriately in language teaching contexts (Bewersdor , Nerdel, et al., [2025;](#informed-consent) Chiu et al., 2024; Pan et al., [2025;](#appendix-survey-items) Promma et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). English language teachers with strong AI literacy are more con dent in their abil- ity to utilize AI, perceive it as useful and manageable, and show greater willingness to accept it in their instructional practice, whereas limited AIL may lead to anxiety or resistance (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Cheng et al., 2025). 

By integrating AIL and Intelligent TPACK within the extended TAM framework, this study aims to explain English language teachers’ acceptance of AI. Speci cally, it investigates how these competencies predict per- ceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and overall, AI acceptance, o ering a comprehensive model for understanding technology adoption in the evolving landscape of English language education. 

### _1.1._ _Statement of the problem_ 

While enthusiasm for AI in education continues to grow, its integration into actual classroom practice remains uneven and context-dependent. In English language teaching, where pedagogy relies heavily on interaction, feedback, and communicative competence, AI presents both transformative opportunities and signi cant challenges. Synthesizing existing research, studies consistently indicate that successful AI adop- tion is not determined solely by teachers’ perceptions of technology, but also by their professional knowl- edge, competencies, and the contextual conditions that support instructional innovation (Li & Manzari, 2025; Mafa & Govender, 2025). This suggests that understanding AI adoption requires moving beyond perception- based models toward more comprehensive frameworks that incorporate both cognitive and pedagogical dimensions. 

However, several critical gaps remain in the literature. First, existing studies applying the TAM have largely focused on general digital technologies rather than AI-speci c tools. For example, studies by Bergdahl and Sjöberg ([2025)](#informed-consent) and Nja et al. (2023), consistently demonstrate that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use predict technology adoption in educational contexts. However, these studies treat technology as a broad construct and do not account for the distinct cognitive, ethical, and adaptive characteristics of AI sys- tems. Similarly, Li and Manzari (2025) argue that AI integration introduces complexities, such as algorithmic decision-making and data-driven feedback, that are not su ciently captured by traditional TAM applications. Taken together, these studies suggest that TAM, in its original form, provides an incomplete explanation of AI adoption. 

Second, while AIL and Intelligent TPACK are increasingly recognized as essential competencies, existing research has examined them in isolation rather than as interconnected constructs. Studies on AI literacy (Chiu et al., 2024; A. Y. Wang, [2022;](#appendix-survey-items) B. Wang et al., [2022)](#appendix-survey-items) emphasize its role in enhancing teachers’ understanding, con dence, and critical evaluation of AI systems. In contrast, studies on AI-related TPACK (Al- Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Cheng et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2024) focus on teachers’ ability to integrate AI into pedagog- ical practice. Although both strands highlight important dimensions of teacher readiness, they remain theoretically and empirically disconnected, limiting understanding of how cognitive readiness or AIL and pedagogical competence or Intelligent TPACK jointly in uence technology acceptance. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 3 

Third, limited research has examined how these competencies interact with core TAM constructs. While some studies suggest that higher levels of digital competence or AI-related knowledge are associated with more positive perceptions of usefulness and ease of use (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Cheng et al., 2025), others focus primarily on direct e ects of TAM variables without incorporating deeper competency-based predictors (Bergdahl & Sjöberg, [2025;](#informed-consent) Nja et al., 2023). This fragmented approach results in a lack of integrated models that explain how professional knowledge and cognitive skills shape PU and PEOU in AI contexts. 

Fourth, the empirical literature is heavily concentrated in technologically advanced and well-resourced settings. Studies conducted in such contexts (Cheng et al., 2025; W. Zhang & Hou, [2024)](#appendix-survey-items) report relatively high levels of technological readiness and institutional support, which may not re ect conditions in developing regions. In contrast, research from resource-constrained environments remains limited, particularly in subject-speci c domains such as English language teaching (Mafa & Govender, 2025). This imbalance restricts the generalizability of existing ndings and leaves important contextual factors underexplored. 

Grounded in the extended TAM, this study seeks to examine how AIL and Intelligent TPACK in uence English language teachers’ acceptance of AI in the Awi Zone of the Amhara Regional State, Ethiopia. The study addresses the following research questions: 

1. To what extent does Intelligent TPACK predict English language teachers’ perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and AI acceptance? 
2. To what extent does Arti cial Intelligence Literacy predict English language teachers’ Intelligent TPACK, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness and AI acceptance? 
3. How do perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use in uence English language teachers’ AI acceptance? 

## 2. Literature review and hypothesis development 

### _2.1._ _Theoretical framework_ 

The integration of AI tools requires not only technological pro ciency but also pedagogical adaptability and ethical awareness. To address these complex dynamics, this study proposes an extended TAM that integrates Intelligent TPACK and AIL as critical antecedents of teachers’ attitudes and BI toward adopting AI in class- room instruction. To avoid conceptual ambiguity, this study adopts the term intelligent TPACK consistently throughout the manuscript. intelligent TPACK is conceptualized as an extension of the traditional TPACK framework, emphasizing the role of arti cial intelligence as a transformative technological domain that reshapes pedagogical strategies and content delivery. Unlike general technological knowledge, AI intro- duces capabilities such as adaptivity, automation, and predictive analytics, which require teachers to develop specialized competencies. 

The TAM remains one of the most in uential frameworks for explaining user acceptance of emerging technologies. According to Davis (1989), PU and PEOU constitute the two primary determinants of BI to use technology. PU re ects the degree to which an individual believes that a system enhances performance, whereas PEOU represents the extent to which using that system is free of e ort (Darayseh, 2023; Davis & Granić, 2024; Galimova et al., 2024). Empirical evidence demonstrates TAM’s robustness in educational set- tings, particularly in predicting technology acceptance among teachers and students (Bergdahl & Sjöberg, [2025;](#informed-consent) W. Zhang & Hou, [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Nonetheless, scholars have criticized TAM for its limited capacity to capture pedagogical and contextual factors in uencing technology integration, especially in relation to complex innovations such as AI (Li & Manzari, 2025). This shortcoming underscores the necessity of combining TAM with models that account for teachers’ professional and contextual competencies. 

Although the TAM provides a robust framework for explaining users’ adoption of technology through PU and PEOU, it does not su ciently account for the domain-speci c competencies required for emerging tech- nologies such as arti cial intelligence. In AI-supported educational contexts, teachers must not only accept the technology but also understand its underlying principles and e ectively integrate it into pedagogical practice. Therefore, this study extends TAM by incorporating AI literacy and intelligent TPACK. AI literacy is conceptualized as a foundational cognitive competency that enables users to comprehend, evaluate, and interact with AI systems, thereby shaping their perceptions of usefulness and ease of use. Meanwhile, intelli- 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

gent TPACK represents teachers’ ability to integrate AI technologies into teaching in pedagogically mean- ingful ways, bridging the gap between technology acceptance and instructional implementation. By integrating these constructs, the proposed model provides a more comprehensive explanation of AI adop- tion in educational settings. 

TPACK conceptualizes the interdependent relationships among content knowledge, pedagogical knowl- edge, and technological knowledge, emphasizing that e ective technology integration emerges from the intersection of these domains (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Recent extensions, such as AI-TPACK, adapt this framework to encompass teachers’ capacity to design, implement, and evaluate instruction using AI-based tools while upholding pedagogical rigor and ethical awareness (Ning et al., 2024). The Intelligent TPACK framework o ers a comprehensive perspective on teachers’ capability to integrate technology e ectively into pedagogy (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Chiu, 2025; Choudhury et al., 2024). Cheng et al. (2025) and Batiibwe and Bakkabulindi ([2016)](#informed-consent) emphasized that Intelligent TPACK not only re ects knowledge integration but also operates as an innovation adoption framework. Li and Manzari (2025) and Mafa and Govender (2025) further identi ed that attitudes and institutional support signi cantly predict successful AI adoption. Within K–12 education, where teachers are navigating accelerated digital transformation, Intelligent TPACK serves as a relevant construct for understanding how professional knowledge and adaptive competence in uence tech- nology acceptance. Importantly, intelligent TPACK is not merely a contextual application of the traditional TPACK framework but represents a conceptual re nement that explicitly incorporates the unique a or- dances of AI technologies. By foregrounding AI-speci c capabilities and their pedagogical implications, intel- ligent TPACK extends beyond general technological integration to capture the evolving nature of teacher competencies in AI-driven educational environments. This distinction enables a more precise understanding of how teachers translate AI-related knowledge into e ective instructional practices. 

AIL extends this theoretical foundation by highlighting the cognitive, technical, and ethical dimensions of AI engagement. It encompasses teachers’ understanding, critical evaluation, and responsible use of AI in educational settings (Pan et al., [2025;](#appendix-survey-items) Promma et al., [2025;](#appendix-survey-items) Xia et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). Tzirides et al. ([2024)](#appendix-survey-items) described AIL as a multidimensional construct integrating technical pro ciency, interpretive capacity, and ethical discern- ment. Teachers with higher AIL are more likely to perceive AI tools as useful and easy to use, thereby devel- oping favorable attitudes toward adoption. Conversely, low AIL may generate uncertainty, ethical concern, or resistance, especially in resource-constrained environments (C. Chen et al., 2024). 

### _2.2._ _Hypothesis development_ 

#### _2.2.1. Intelligent technological pedagogical content knowledge (intelligent TPACK)_ 

Intelligent TPACK represents teachers’ integrated understanding of how technology, pedagogy, and content interact to support e ective teaching and learning (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Batiibwe & Bakkabulindi, [2016)](#informed-consent). It re ects a teacher’s capacity to meaningfully embed technological tools within subject-speci c instruction while maintaining pedagogical coherence. In the evolving landscape of AI integration, Intelligent TPACK has been extended into the Intelligent TPACK framework, encompassing educators’ competence to apply AI technologies to enhance instruction and address student learning challenges (Karataş & Ataç, 2024; Ning et al., 2024). Teachers with strong Intelligent TPACK tend to perceive new technologies as easier to use and more aligned with instructional goals, thereby increasing their technological self-e cacy and innovation adoption readiness (Cheng et al., 2025; Li & Manzari, 2025). 

Empirical evidence underscores the in uence of Intelligent TPACK on PEOU, as teachers who possess the necessary pedagogical and technological integration skills tend to nd digital tools less complex to operate (Al-Abdullatif, [2024)](#informed-consent). Intelligent TPACK also enhances PU, as teachers recognize how AI applications can improve learning e ciency and pedagogical outcomes (Tan et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). Furthermore, Intelligent TPACK positively shapes attitudes toward technology by fostering con dence and openness to digital innovation, which in turn strengthens teachers’ BI to adopt AI-based tools (An et al., [2022;](#informed-consent) Mafa & Govender, 2025). Although some studies have reported mixed results regarding Intelligent TPACK direct in uence on PU (Al- Abdullatif, [2024)](#informed-consent), the cumulative evidence suggests its multidimensional impact across perceptual and behavioral outcomes. As presented in Figure 1, this study posits the following hypotheses: 

**H1:** Intelligent TPACK signi cantly predicts PEOU. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 5 

**H2:** Intelligent TPACK signi cantly predicts PU. 

**H3:** Intelligent TPACK signi cantly predicts BI. 

#### _2.2.2._ _AI literacy_ 

AIL encompasses teachers’ ability to understand, critically evaluate, and e ectively apply arti cial intelli- gence technologies in educational contexts (Philippakos & Rocconi, [2025;](#appendix-survey-items) B. Wang et al., [2022)](#appendix-survey-items). It involves technical pro ciency, ethical discernment, and the capacity to engage responsibly with AI systems in teach- ing and learning (Pan et al., [2025;](#appendix-survey-items) Xia et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). AI-literate educators can leverage intelligent tools for adaptive instruction, assessment automation, and data-informed pedagogy, thereby expanding their AI- TPACK (Celik, [2023;](#informed-consent) Sperling et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). This literacy enables teachers to integrate AI within their AI-TPACK framework, fostering innovation and re ective practice (Al-Abdullatif, [2024)](#informed-consent). 

Empirical ndings con rm that AIL positively in uences PEOU and PU. S. Zhang ([2024)](#appendix-survey-items) reported that AI- literate teachers face fewer technological barriers and perceive AI systems as easier to operate, while Pan et al. ([2025)](#appendix-survey-items) found a direct positive association between AIL and PU in educational enhancement. AIL also shapes teachers’ attitudes toward AI, with Bewersdor , Hornberger, et al. ([2025)](#informed-consent) noting that educators with higher AIL express more con dence and positivity toward AI adoption. Additionally, research shows indirect and direct e ects of AIL on BI, mediated by PEOU, PU, and attitude (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Schiavo et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Accordingly, this study posits the following hypotheses: 

**H4:** AIL signi cantly predicts Intelligent TPACK 

**H5**: AIL signi cantly predicts PEOU. 

**H6**: AIL signi cantly predicts PU. 

**H7:** AIL signi cantly predicts BI. 

#### _2.2.3._ _Perceived usefulness \[PU\]_ 

PU refers to the degree to which an individual believes that using a particular technology enhances perfor- mance and e ectiveness in completing speci c tasks (Davis, 1989). In educational settings, PU re ects teachers’ perceptions of how AI supports instructional e ciency, learning outcomes, and decision-making (Pan et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). Empirical evidence indicates that PU is one of the strongest predictors of BI to use tech- nology (Pan et al., [2025;](#appendix-survey-items) Teo et al., [2012)](#appendix-survey-items). Nja et al. (2023) con rmed that PU strongly predicted BI to use AI. PU also mediates the in uence of cognitive and a ective factors such as AIL and attitude translating beliefs into BI (Wu et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Accordingly, this study proposes that, 

**H8**: PU signi cantly predicts BI. 

#### _2.2.4._ _Perceived ease of use \[PEOU\]_ 

PEOU is de ned as the extent to which an individual believes that using a technology will be free of e ort (Davis, 1989). In the context of AI integration, PEOU captures teachers’ perceptions of the simplicity and user- friendliness of AI tools employed in teaching and learning (Schiavo et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Prior studies consistently show that educators who nd AI systems intuitive and less demanding demonstrate greater BI to use them (Hazzan-Bishara et al., 2025; Zhang & Hou, [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). PEOU not only directly predicts BI but also enhances PU by shaping teachers’ judgments of AI’s overall value and applicability (Pan et al., [2025)](#appendix-survey-items). Teachers with high PEOU perceive AI as more useful, thereby reinforcing their willingness to adopt it (Nja et al., 2023). Accordingly, this study posits that, 

**H9:** PEOU signi cantly predicts PU. 

**H10:** PEOU signi cantly predicts BI.

## 3. Methods and materials 

### _3.1._ _Participants_ 

The participants were K–12 English language teachers from the Awi Administration Zone in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia. Due to regional con ict and limited resources for in-person data collection, a conve- nience sampling approach was employed, supported by online recruitment strategies to ensure accessibility and participant safety. 

Participants were recruited through multiple professional and communication platforms commonly used by English language teachers in the region. Speci cally, invitations to participate in the study were dissemi- nated via Telegram groups, Facebook Messenger groups, group email lists, and professional networks. In addition, the survey link was shared via text messages (SMS) with teachers whose phone numbers were obtained from o cial repositories of the concerned educational bodies. These platforms and contact sources were selected because they are widely used for professional communication and information sharing among teachers in the study area. The survey link was accompanied by a brief description of the study purpose, eligibility criteria, and participation instructions. In some cases, group administrators and key contacts facili- tated the distribution of the survey link to enhance outreach. 

An initial invitation was shared with approximately 400 teachers across these platforms. Of these, 360 participants completed the online questionnaire, yielding a response rate of approximately 90%. To ensure relevance, the inclusion criteria required participants to be currently practicing K–12 English language teach- ers in either public or private schools within the Awi Administration Zone. 

Participation was entirely voluntary, and informed consent was obtained electronically prior to survey completion. The survey was administered through an online platform, allowing participants to respond at their convenience while maintaining anonymity and safety in a context where face-to-face data collection was not feasible. 

As presented in [Table 1 ](#table-2-results-of-measurement-model-assessment)below of the 360 respondents, 223 (61.9%) were male and 137 (38.1%) were female, re ecting the gender distribution commonly reported in regional teaching populations. In terms of age distribution, the largest proportion of participants (40.3%) were between 21 and 30 years old, followed by 33.9% who were below 20 years. Teachers aged 31–40 years comprised 13.6% of the sample, while those aged 41–50 years and 51 years and above represented 10.6% and 1.7%, respectively. Regarding teaching experience, more than half of the respondents (51.7%) had 1–10 years of classroom experience. Teachers with 11–15 years and 16–20 years of experience represented 27.2% and 16.4%, respectively, while 4.7% had 21–25 years of experience. 

### _3.2._ _Instruments_ 

The study examined participants’ perceptions across six key constructs derived from the proposed research model, using a previously validated survey instrument consisting of 26 items. The questionnaire began with a section on demographic information, followed by the assessment of the six latent constructs. Each con- struct was measured using a ve-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 =strongly agree, allowing participants to indicate the extent of their agreement with each statement. 

The constructs measured included PU and PEOU, each assessed through four items adapted from Davis (1989)’ original TAM instrument. The construct of GenAI Acceptance (four items) was also drawn from TAM, re ecting behavioral intention toward AI adoption in instructional settings. Intelligent TPACK was evaluated using six items adapted from Celik ([2023)](#informed-consent), which emphasize teachers’ capacity to integrate arti cial intelli- gence tools into pedagogical practice e ectively. 

AI literacy is widely recognized as a multidimensional construct encompassing cognitive, technical, and ethical dimensions. However, this study adopts a parsimonious approach by measuring AI literacy using four items adapted from Al-Abdullatif ([2024)](#informed-consent), focusing on core competencies relevant to teachers’ interaction with AI in educational settings. This approach aligns with prior research suggesting that shorter, well- validated scales can provide reliable and valid measurement when they capture the essential aspects of a construct (Hair et al., 2019). The scale demonstrated satisfactory reliability and convergent validity (_α_ = .87, _CR_ = .92, _AVE_ = .63), supporting its adequacy for the purposes of this study. The instrument was reviewed for content validity by experts in educational technology and English language teaching prior to deployment.

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 7 

Minor revisions were made to ensure clarity, contextual relevance, and alignment with the Ethiopian K–12 educational context (see Appendix). 

### _3.3._ _Measurement reliability and validity_ 

Measurement reliability and validity were evaluated prior to testing the structural model, following estab- lished guidelines for covariance-based structural equation modeling. Internal consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability coe cients. Cronbach’s alpha values of.70 or higher were considered indicative of acceptable reliability, while composite reliability values exceeding.70 were used to con rm construct reliability (Raykov, [1997)](#appendix-survey-items). Convergent validity was examined through stan- dardized factor loadings and average variance extracted. Factor loadings equal to or greater than.70 were regarded as satisfactory, and AVE values exceeding .50 were interpreted as evidence that the latent con- structs accounted for a substantial proportion of variance in their observed indicators (Fornell & Larcker, 1981; Hair et al., 2019). Discriminant validity was assessed using the Fornell–Larcker criterion, whereby the square root of each construct’s AVE was compared with its inter-construct correlations, with adequate discriminant validity inferred when the square root of AVE exceeded the corresponding correlations (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). 

### _3.4._ _Data analysis_ 

This study employed covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) using AMOS to test the pro- posed research model. CB-SEM was selected because it is well suited for theory testing and con rmation, allowing for the simultaneous estimation of relationships among latent constructs while accounting for measurement error (Hair et al., 2019; Kline, 2016). Unlike variance-based approaches such as PLS-SEM, which are more appropriate for exploratory or prediction-oriented research, CB-SEM is recommended when the objective is to validate an established theoretical framework, such as the extended TAM used in this study (Hair et al., 2019). Furthermore, CB-SEM provides comprehensive model t indices, enabling rigorous assess- ment of how well the proposed model ts the observed data (Byrne, [2016)](#informed-consent). 

In addition, potential common method bias was assessed to ensure the validity of the ndings. Following the recommendations of Podsako et al. ([2003)](#appendix-survey-items), Harman’s single-factor test was conducted to examine whether a single factor accounted for the majority of variance in the data. The results indicated that no sin- gle factor dominated, suggesting that common method bias was unlikely to be a serious concern. Proce- dural remedies, such as ensuring anonymity and reducing evaluation apprehension, were also implemented during data collection to minimize potential bias (Podsako et al., [2003)](#appendix-survey-items). 

## 4. Result 

### _4.1._ _Measurement model assessment_ 

Before testing the structural relationships, the reliability and validity of the measurement model were exam- ined. [Table 2 ](#table-2-results-of-measurement-model-assessment)presents the results of this assessment, including standardized factor loadings, Cronbach’s alpha _(α),_ _CR,_ _AVE_, inter-construct correlations, and Heterotrait–Monotrait (HTMT) ratios. All indicators loaded strongly on their intended latent constructs, with standardized factor loadings ranging from .725 to .917, exceeding the recommended threshold of .70 and demonstrating adequate indicator reliability (Hair et al., 2019). Internal consistency reliability was con rmed, as Cronbach’s alpha values ranged from .871 to .920 and CR values from .872 to .918, both above the suggested cuto of.70 (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Sathyanarayana & Mohanasundaram, [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Convergent validity was also supported, with AVE values ranging from.631 to.738, surpassing the recommended minimum of.50 (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). 

Discriminant validity was evaluated using both the Fornell–Larcker criterion and HTMT ratios. As shown in [Table 2,](#table-2-results-of-measurement-model-assessment) the square roots of the AVE (_bolded_ _diagonal_ _values_) were greater than the corresponding inter- construct correlations, and all HTMT ratios were below the conservative threshold of 0.85, con rming satisfactory discriminant validity (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). Collectively, these results indicate that the 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

measurement model demonstrates strong reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, providing a sound basis for subsequent structural model analysis. 

### _4.2._ _Con_ _rmatory factor analysis_ 

Con rmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted to assess the construct validity of the measurement model comprising ve latent variables: AI Literacy, Intelligent TPACK, PEOU, PU, and AI Acceptance. As indicated in [Table 3 ](#table-2-results-of-measurement-model-assessment)the initial model (CFA1) indicated suboptimal t, _χ2_ (199) = 596.94, _χ2/df_ = 3.00, _CFI_ = .929, _TLI_ = .918, _RMSEA_ = .075, _SRMR_ = .050. Based on modi cation indices, selected error terms were correlated to improve model speci cation (see[ Figure 2)](#42-con-rmatory-factor-analysis). The modi ed model (CFA2) demonstrated a signi cantly better t: _χ2_ (197) = 445.59, _χ2/df_ = 2.26, _CFI_ = .956, _TLI_ = .948, _RMSEA_ = .059, _SRMR_ = .053. These values meet the recommended thresholds (_CFI_ and _TLI_ \> .95, _RMSEA_ \< .06, _SRMR_ \< .08), suggesting that the revised model provides a good representation of the observed data (Hu & Bentler, 1999). 

### _4.3._ _Structural model analysis and hypothesis testing_ 

The path analysis investigates how AI literacy and Intelligent TPACK in uence English teachers’ acceptance of AI, both directly and indirectly, through PEOU and PU. The model is consistent with the extended TAM, which posits that technology-related knowledge and perceptions of usefulness and ease of use are key determi- nants of technology acceptance among English teachers. 

As indicated in [Table 4,](#5-discussion) AI Literacy signi cantly predicted Intelligent TPACK (β = .236, _SE_ = .058, _CR_ = 4.078, _p_ \< .001), indicating that teachers with higher AI literacy tend to possess more integrated technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge for AI use in teaching. In turn, Intelligent TPACK exerted a positive e ect on PEOU (β = .181, _SE_ = .056, _CR_ = 3.213, _p_ = .001), suggesting that teachers with stronger intelligent TPACK nd AI tools easier to operate. 

Similarly, AI Literacy directly and positively in uenced PEOU (β = .320, _SE_ = .059, _CR_ = 5.426, _p_ \< .001). Intelligent TPACK also demonstrated a modest but signi cant impact on perceived usefulness (β = .125, _SE_ = . 056, _CR_ = 2.230, _p_ = .026). PEOU emerged as a strong and signi cant predictor of PU (β = .451, _SE_ = .067, _CR_ = 6.777, _p_ \< .001), con rming the core assumption of the TAM. 

However, the results indicated that H6, the in uence of AI Literacy on PU, was not supported (β = .055, _p_ = . 348). This suggests that although AI literacy enhances teachers’ understanding of AI, it does not directly in uence their perception of its instructional usefulness. Instead, perceived usefulness may depend more on teachers’ ability to integrate AI into pedagogical practice, as re ected in Intelligent TPACK. This implies that AI literacy may exert an indirect e ect rather than a direct in uence on perceived usefulness. Similarly, H10, the in uence of PEOU on AI Acceptance, was not supported (β = −.036, _p_ = .564). While perceived ease of use is a core component of TAM, this nding suggests it may be less critical in the context of AI adoption. Teach- ers may prioritize the pedagogical value and e ectiveness of AI tools over their ease of use, particularly

## 5. Discussion 

The ndings reveal a structured relationship among AI literacy, Intelligent TPACK, PEOU, PU, and English teachers’ AI acceptance, o ering important theoretical and practical insights into AI adoption. Rather than acting independently, these factors operate as a competence–perception system, where teachers’ knowl- edge and skills shape how they evaluate and adopt AI technologies. 

First, the signi cant e ect of AI literacy on Intelligent TPACK suggests that technical understanding serves as a foundation for pedagogical integration rather than an end in itself. This aligns with prior research indi- cating that teachers’ ability to meaningfully use AI depends on both their understanding of AI systems and their capacity to integrate them into instructional practice (Celik, [2023;](#informed-consent) Ning et al., 2024; K. Wang et al., [2024)](#appendix-survey-items). Synthesizing these ndings, AI literacy can be interpreted as an enabling condition that supports the devel- opment of higher-order pedagogical competencies, reinforcing the idea that e ective AI use is fundamen- tally pedagogical rather than purely technical. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 11 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Figure 3.** Final Structural path model standardized regression weights. 

Second, the nding that AI literacy and Intelligent TPACK signi cantly predict PEOU, and indirectly in uence PU, suggests that PEOU are shaped by underlying competencies. Consistent with prior studies (Al- Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) An et al., [2022;](#informed-consent) Firdaus et al., 2025), teachers who possess stronger knowledge and integra- tion skills are more likely to perceive AI tools as manageable and bene cial. Taken together, these studies indicate that TAM constructs in AI contexts are not merely subjective perceptions but are partially grounded in teachers’ preparedness and experience. This extends TAM by suggesting that PEOU re ects not only sys- tem characteristics but also users’ competence. 

However, the non-signi cant direct e ect of PEOU on AI acceptance indicates a shift in the role of usabil- ity in advanced technology contexts. While traditional TAM studies emphasize the importance of PEOU, recent research shows mixed ndings, with some studies reporting a diminished direct e ect in more com- plex or innovative technologies (Alshammari & Al-Mamary, [2025;](#informed-consent) Mustofa et al., 2025), while others still nd it signi cant in more general contexts (Nja et al., 2023). In this study, the nding suggests that teachers may be willing to engage with AI tools even if they are not easy to use, provided they o er clear instructional bene ts. This reinforces the interpretation that PEOU primarily operates indirectly through PU rather than as a direct determinant of acceptance. 

Third, the strong e ect of PU on AI acceptance con rms that perceived instructional value is the central driver of adoption decisions. This is consistent with a broad body of research showing that usefulness remains the most robust predictor of technology acceptance across educational contexts (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Firdaus et al., 2025; Ning et al., 2024; Oved & Alt, 2025). However, the relatively smaller direct e ect of AI literacy suggests that knowledge alone is insu cient to drive adoption unless it translates into perceived value. Synthesizing these ndings, it can be argued that AI literacy in uences acceptance primarily through its impact on Intelligent TPACK and PU. 

Overall, these ndings extend the traditional TAM by demonstrating that AI acceptance is not solely perception-driven but competence-dependent. By integrating AI literacy and Intelligent TPACK, the study highlights how cognitive readiness and pedagogical capability shape teachers’ perceptions and ultimately their adoption decisions. This supports emerging perspectives that call for expanding TAM to include domain-speci c competencies in order to better explain technology use in complex and evolving contexts (Al-Abdullatif, [2024;](#informed-consent) Ning et al., 2024). 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

### _5.1._ _Theoretical implications_ 

This study extends the TAM by integrating AI literacy and Intelligent TPACK to explain English language teachers’ acceptance of AI. The results demonstrate that these constructs jointly enhance the predictive power of TAM by linking cognitive and pedagogical competencies with PU, PEOU, and AI acceptance. More- over, positioning AI literacy as a direct antecedent of Intelligent TPACK clari es how conceptual, technical, and ethical knowledge of AI contributes to teachers’ ability to integrate AI pedagogically. Finally, the stronger predictive role of PU compared to PEOU reinforces the idea that teachers adopt AI primarily for its instructional value rather than simplicity. 

### _5.2._ _Practical implications_ 

From a practical perspective, the ndings suggest that professional development should move beyond basic technical training and focus on integrating AI into pedagogical practice. Studies consistently show that train- ing programs that combine technical understanding with instructional application are more e ective in pro- moting meaningful technology adoption (Celik, [2023;](#informed-consent) Chan & Tang, [2024;](#informed-consent) Sun et al., [2022)](#appendix-survey-items). Therefore, enhancing both AI literacy and Intelligent TPACK is likely to have the greatest impact on teachers’ percep- tions of usefulness and their willingness to adopt AI in the classroom. 

First, teacher education programs should integrate structured AI literacy modules covering technical con- cepts, ethics, and critical evaluation to build the foundation for Intelligent TPACK. Second, professional devel- opment should focus on pedagogical applications of AI, such as lesson design, feedback, and assessment, rather than tool demonstrations. Third, school leaders should highlight the concrete bene ts of AI, since PU remains the strongest driver of acceptance. Finally, ethical and policy frameworks on data privacy, integrity, and bias must accompany AI initiatives to ensure responsible implementation. 

### _5.3._ _Limitations and future directions_ 

This study has several limitations. First, it focuses on English language teachers in the Awi Zone of Ethiopia, which may limit generalizability to other contexts or subjects. Second, the cross-sectional design prevents causal inference, capturing only associations at a single point in time. Longitudinal studies could better examine how AI literacy and Intelligent TPACK evolve. Third, reliance on self-reported data may introduce common method bias or social desirability e ects, and future research could incorporate observations or system-based measures. Fourth, convenience sampling and online recruitment may overrepresent techno- logically inclined teachers, limiting representativeness. Finally, factors such as institutional readiness, AI self- e cacy, and ethical attitudes were not included and may further explain AI adoption. 

## 6. Conclusion 

This study examined the relationships among AI literacy, Intelligent TPACK, PEOU, PU, and teachers’ AI accep- tance. The structural model indicates that AI literacy exerts a signi cant positive in uence on Intelligent TPACK, PEOU, and AI acceptance, highlighting literacy as a foundational competency for engaging with generative AI tools. Intelligent TPACK, in turn, signi cantly predicts PEOU, PU, and AI acceptance, under- scoring the importance of pedagogical technological integration for teachers’ technology acceptance rather than technical skills alone. PEOU signi cantly predicts PU, consistent with the Technology Acceptance Model, although its direct path to acceptance is not signi cant in this context. PU strongly predicts AI acceptance and partially mediates the e ects of Intelligent TPACK and PEOU on AI acceptance. Overall, the model sug- gests that teachers’ AI acceptance is shaped by a combination of AI literacy, Intelligent TPACK, and PU of AI, rather than by PEOU alone.

## Informed consent 

All participants were fully informed about the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of their participation, and their right to withdraw at any time without penalty. Informed consent was obtained electronically from all participants before they completed the survey. 

## Ethical approval 

Ethical clearance for this study was obtained from the Ethical Review Board of Injibara University, Ethiopia. The research protocol was reviewed and approved in accordance with the university’s ethical guidelines for studies involving human participants. 

## Use of arti cial intelligence 

Arti cial intelligence (AI) tools were used exclusively for language editing and proofreading purposes. The authors main- tained full control over the content, analysis, interpretation, and conclusions of the study.

### Appendix. Survey items 

Construct (items) Perceived ease of use 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

1. Learning how to use GenAI tools is easy for me. 
2. My interaction with GenAI tools is clear and simple. 
3. I nd GenAI tools easy to use for my teaching. 
4. It is easy for me to become skillful in using GenAI tools. 

Perceived usefulness 

1. I nd GenAI tools useful for performing my teaching duties. 
2. Using GenAI tools increases my chances of achieving high job performance. 
3. Using GenAI tools helps me accomplish my teaching tasks e ortlessly. 
4. Using GenAI tools increases my productivity. 

AI literacy 

1. I can use AI applications or products to improve my work e ciency. 
2. I can evaluate the capabilities and limitations of an AI application or product after using it for a while. 
3. I always comply with ethical principles when using AI applications or products. 
4. I am alert to privacy and information security issues when using AI applications or products. 

Intelligent TPACK 

1. In teaching English, I know how to use di erent GenAI tools for adaptive and real-time feedback 
2. In teaching English, I know how to use di erent GenAI tools for personalized learning. 
3. In teaching English, I know how to use di erent GenAI tools for generate quiz and assessments. 
4. I can teach English lessons that appropriately combine my teaching content, GenAI tools, and teaching strategies. 
5. I can take a leadership role among my colleagues in the integration of GenAI tools into our teaching eld. 
6. I can select various GenAI tools to monitor students’ learning in my teaching process. 

GenAI acceptance 

1. I look forward to use GenAI tools in my teaching. 
2. I intend to use GenAI tools in my future teaching. 
3. I plan to use GenAI tools in my future teaching. 
4. I support the adoption of GenAI tools in teaching English
